description: Hi! I have a background in physics and astronomy, with experience in Python, scientific data analysis, and problem-solving. I'm interested in exploring astronomical data and building a tool that makes it easier for people to discover interesting objects in the sky.
summary:
The SPHEREx Time-Lapse Viewer is a public web tool for exploring how the infrared sky changes over time. Users can enter sky coordinates, search by object name, or select a preset challenge target. The app retrieves SPHEREx image cutouts from NASA’s Infrared Science Archive (IRSA), aligns observations of the same region, and presents them as a playable time-lapse, a frame grid, and an early-versus-late difference image.

The viewer addresses the Planet X and SPHEREx challenge by making it easier to compare observations taken on different dates. Students, volunteers, and other users can look for objects that appear to shift against the background sky and flag candidates for follow-up. As SPHEREx continues to survey the infrared sky, the viewer gives more people a way to help inspect those observations directly from a browser.
details:
What it does and how it works

Users can choose a preset challenge target, search for an object by name, or enter right ascension and declination in decimal degrees or sexagesimal format. The app queries the NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive (IRSA), downloads small SPHEREx cutouts around the selected region, aligns the images on a common north-up grid, and subtracts the estimated background.

Users can play the observations in chronological order, compare individual images in a frame grid, or inspect a difference image made from combined early and late observations. When proper-motion information is available, the app uses it to predict the target’s position at each observation date. A red ring marks that predicted position in the frame grid. The Frame info tab gives users access to observation metadata, and demo mode can reuse previously processed frames when a matching set is available.

Benefits and intended impact

The viewer lets students, volunteers, and amateur astronomers explore SPHEREx observations without writing code or downloading full images. Bringing the time-lapse, frame grid, and difference image together lets users spot a possible change, inspect the individual observations, and decide whether it warrants follow-up.

Tools and technologies

The app was built in Python with Streamlit, Astropy, Astroquery, Reproject, Matplotlib, NumPy, and pandas. It accesses SPHEREx data through IRSA and is hosted on Streamlit Community Cloud, with source code on GitHub.

Design choices and factors considered

Downloading cutouts limits data transfer, and users can adjust the field of view and choose which SPHEREx detectors to include. A wider field can help keep faster-moving targets in view, with longer load times. Presets give first-time users a place to start and cover the five targets named in the challenge brief: Barnard’s Star, Epsilon Indi B, WISE 0855, RW Aurigae, and R Draconis.
